This is a smooth, enjoyable read and a moving and often amusing account of JD Vance's chaotic and difficult childhood in a 'lower class' family. At the same time, it alerts us that upward social mobility in America may not be what it once was. One of the things that made America as a young country so vibrant was the possibility of any individual rising, within one generation, from the lowest economic class to the elite. JD Vance's own case proves that this possibility still exists, yet he points out that had he not been very lucky at several stages, he might have remained trapped in a world of social problems and low ambition. In the current conditions, too many of the youngest generation in the 'working class' are doomed by a traumatic childhood and a lack of perspective and good example, and for the country as a whole this leads to an enormous waste of talent and energy. A healthy social mobility based on potential, merit and yes, some amount of luck, benefits an entire nation including its elite.
